extracted.intended_audience: students, readers, and writers of fiction; literary critics
extracted.subtask_description: Criteria for recognizing and judging two novelistic aspects — fantasy and prophecy — including devices, tone, reader requirements, and stylistic effects, illustrated with examples (Tristram Shandy, Flecker’s Magic, Zuleika Dobson, Ulysses, Dostoevsky, George Eliot, Melville).

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of fantasy
rubrics_metrics.description: “It implies the supernatural, but need not express it.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Fantasy is defined primarily by implication of the supernatural rather than explicit supernatural explanation. The writer may avoid literal explanations and rely on the sense that something beyond ordinary causation is present.

rubrics_metrics.name: Devices of the fantastist
rubrics_metrics.description: “the introduction of a god, ghost, angel, monkey, monster, midget, witch into ordinary life; or the introduction of ordinary men into no man’s land, the future, the past, the interior of the earth, the fourth dimension; or divings into and dividings of personality; or finally the device of parody or adaptation.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These are the principal stock devices available to fantasy writers. The page notes their number is ‘strictly limited’ but they can be put to fresh use. Use examples (ring-wishes, flying motor-bus, mythological borrowings) to show how devices may be reinvented. Recognize device-limits when assessing originality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Economy and freshness of device application
rubrics_metrics.description: “These devices need never grow stale; they will occur naturally to writers of a certain temperament, and be put to fresh use; but the fact that their number is strictly limited is of interest; and suggests that the beam of light can only be manipulated in certain ways.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether the author reuses familiar fantasy devices creatively rather than mechanically. Anti-pattern: relying on stock device without imaginative recombination so that fantasy feels derivative.

rubrics_metrics.name: Socratic method and building tension
rubrics_metrics.description: “It proceeds with a growing tension, a series of little shocks. The method is Socratic.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess narrative technique that leads the reader through incremental discoveries or objections (Socratic questioning) to create escalating tension. Example: Flecker’s Magic moving from simple wishes to increasingly fraught permutations. Positive sign: mounting small shocks; negative sign: flat progression.

rubrics_metrics.name: Character definiteness as engagement
rubrics_metrics.description: “His character, though slightly sketched, is individual, and this definiteness causes the book to grip.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even in fantasy, distinct, individualized characters (even sketched briefly) increase reader engagement. Score positively when characters feel particular and motivate plot; score negatively if characters are clichés or indistinct masks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Language that bridges magic and common sense
rubrics_metrics.description: “the mark of the true fantasist—does Norman Matson merge the kingdoms of magic and common sense by using words that apply to both, and the mixture he has created comes alive.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Look for diction and phrasing that are simultaneously credible in ordinary reality and in the supernatural world. This double-applicability (words that ‘apply to both’) enlivens the fantasy. Anti-pattern: language that fits only one register and jars in the other.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriateness of mythological/adapted frameworks
rubrics_metrics.description: “Parody or adaptation have enormous advantages ... an already existing book or literary tradition may inspire them—they may find high up in its cornices a pattern that will serve as a beginning ...”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate how well a writer borrows or adapts an earlier mythology or work: does it serve as a useful framework or feel forced? Examples: Fielding (false start), The Magic Flute (successful adaptation), Joyce’s use of the Odyssey (guiding framework). Consider whether adaptation helps authors who struggle to create characters.

rubrics_metrics.name: Misuse of supernatural machinery
rubrics_metrics.description: “To have entrusted Zuleika to one of them would be inept; the fantasy would become heavy or thin.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judge whether a chosen supernatural mechanism suits the tone and scale of the work. If the device is ill-fitting it can make the work feel either ponderous (heavy) or insubstantial (thin).

rubrics_metrics.name: Prophecy defined as a tone of voice
rubrics_metrics.description: “Prophecy—in our sense of foretelling the future we have no concern... His theme is the universe... he proposes to sing, and the strangeness of song arising in the halls of fiction is bound to give us a shock.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat prophetic writing as an overarching tonal quality rather than literal prediction: it is an ‘accent’ or song that pervades diction, sentence-turns, and viewpoint. When evaluating prophetic fiction focus on voice and tonal sweep more than plot plausibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reader qualities required for prophetic fiction
rubrics_metrics.description: “The prophetic aspect demands two qualities: humility and the suspension of the sense of humour.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess reception conditions: prophetic novels ask readers to surrender ironic distance and to approach with humility; failure to do so may lead readers to laugh at the prophet and miss the intended effect. This is guidance for critics/readers rather than writers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prophetic fiction: reach and universality
rubrics_metrics.description: “He is a great novelist in the ordinary sense... he has also the greatness of a prophet... the extension, the melting, the unity through love and pity occur in a region which can only be implied... Mitya is—all of us.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A prophetic novelist creates characters who ‘extend’ beyond their particular circumstances to imply universal human truths; judge whether characters function as particular individuals and as vehicles for wider implication simultaneously. Positive sign: characters that summon the universal without losing individuality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prophetic fiction: spasmodic realism and intermittent foreground detail
rubrics_metrics.description: “It is spasmodically realistic. ... Little things in the foreground seem to be all that the prophet cares about at moments—he sits down with them so quiet and busy like a child.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate the work for sudden, intense realism: minute, accurate foreground detail punctuating visionary stretches. This intermittent realism can illuminate the prophetic voice; look for catalogues or precise scenes amid larger tonal sweep.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prophetic fiction: sensation of song and rough surface
rubrics_metrics.description: “It gives us the sensation of a song or of sound... roughness of surface... full of dents and grooves and lumps and spikes which draw from us little cries of approval and disapproval. When they have past, the roughness is forgotten, they become as smooth as the moon.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether the prose creates a musical, sung effect and whether apparent roughness (unevenness, interruptions) contributes to a lasting aesthetic harmony. Roughness during reading can be a virtue if the after-effect is unifying and memorable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Contrast prophet vs preacher (different effects of similar subject-matter)
rubrics_metrics.description: “The first writer is a preacher, and the second a prophet... George Eliot talks about God, but never alters her focus; God and the tables and chairs are all in the same plane... In Dostoevsky the characters and situations always stand for more than themselves; infinity attends them.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When comparing authors, distinguish a ‘preacher’ (keeps moral focus local and coherent, treats divine presence within the same frame as ordinary objects) from a ‘prophet’ (whose characters imply the infinite). Use this dichotomy to explain differences in reader response and the scope of implication.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prophet's anti-method: song not reflection or hammering
rubrics_metrics.description: “A prophet does not reflect. And he does not hammer away... A prophet does not reflect. And he does not hammer away. That is why we exclude Joyce... it is talk, talk, never song.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether the work aims for ‘song’ (intuitive, tonal, non-argumentative) rather than sustained philosophical reflection or relentless argumentation. Anti-patterns: overworked, laborious undermining of the universe (named as Joyce’s ‘workmanlike’ approach here) which substitutes talk for song.
